qt: to the Commission Stelios Kouloglou (The Left) Subject:

The bill proposed by the Greek Government for the reform of the judicial system in Greece – which involves getting rid of all the country’s district courts and merging them with the first instance courts in the seat of each regional unit1, adding further obstacles to what is an already inefficient justice system – is part of a bigger plan which makes access to justice harder and more expensive, while plans to privatise certain judicial functions would disproportionately benefit big law firms. According to a number of bodies234, the changes will force citizens, lawyers and court staff to travel long distances and will make access to justice harder for many, without speeding up the administration of justice in any way. The ratio of judges to court clerks in the EU is almost 1:3 whereas in Greece it is 1:1. Public spending on justice is on average EUR 65 per EU resident while in Greece it is just EUR 42, placing the country bottom of the list5. The needs of the majority of citizens with regard to access to justice are being overlooked under the pretext of ‘saving resources’. At the same time, justice sector staff are facing serious challenges such as the prospect of having to work a long distance from where they live. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: How far, in its estimation, are the measures aligned with the goals of the Recovery and Resilience Facility, especially as regards the effective use of funds for ensuring equal access to justice for all EU citizens?
at: (English version) to the Commission Stelios Kouloglou (The Left) (25 April 2024) Subject: Greek government’s decision to merge first instance courts unsettles workers and makes it harder to access judicial services The bill proposed by the Greek Government for the reform of the judicial system in Greece — which involves getting rid of all the country’s district courts and merging them with the first instance courts in the seat of each regional unit (1), adding further obstacles to what is an already inefficient justice system — is part of a bigger plan which makes access to justice harder and more expensive, while plans to privatise certain judicial functions would disproportionately benefit big law firms. According to a number of bodies (2) (3) (4), the changes will force citizens, lawyers and court staff to travel long distances and will make access to justice harder for many, without speeding up the administration of justice in any way. The ratio of judges to court clerks in the EU is almost 1:3 whereas in Greece it is 1:1. Public spending on justice is on average EUR 65 per EU resident while in Greece it is just EUR 42, placing the country bottom of the list (5). The needs of the majority of citizens with regard to access to justice are being overlooked under the pretext of ‘saving resources’. At the same time, justice sector staff are facing serious challenges such as the prospect of having to work a long distance from where they live. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: How far, in its estimation, are the measures aligned with the goals of the Recovery and Resilience Facility, especially as regards the effective use of funds for ensuring equal access to justice for all EU citizens? (15 July 2024) As part of the Justice reforms under the Greek Recovery and Resilience Plan, Greece is undertaking a revision of the judicial map and adopted law 5108/2024 (6). This judicial map revision, alongside a previous revision of the administrative judicial map enacted in 2023, is part of a wider reform aiming at accelerating the administration of justice. According to the Greek authorities, the revision of the judicial map is expected to accelerate the processing of cases, resulting in a reduction of the case disposition time at second instance to 550 days down from the current average of approximately 1400 days for civil and commercial cases (7). Under Cohesion Policy, the Digital Transformation programme will also contribute to the modernization and digital upgrade of the Greek Justice system.
